summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The common-law offence of sodomy was struck down in 2012, and male same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since; sexual activity between women was never criminalised. A joint stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho records same-sex conduct as lawful while documenting the absence of protections.

No general anti-discrimination statute protects LGBTIQ+ people. The Labour Act 2024, the current statutory framework for workplace rights, bans employment discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation and defines workplace gender-based violence and harassment as violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, directed at workers, trainees, probationers, applicants, managers, supervisors, customers, clients, suppliers or contractors because of sex, gender or gender identity, or affecting persons of a particular sex, gender or gender identity disproportionately. Section 127(4) of the Children's Protection and Welfare Act 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination based on sexual orientation in the selection of a diversion programme, process or option for a child. Since 2013 the Credit Reporting Regulations have barred credit bureaus from holding sexual-orientation information except where it is self-evident from a person's marital status and family member list. None of these provisions supplies a general equality guarantee, and the inventory does not state that the Labour Act's discrimination clause extends to gender identity.

The October 2024 joint stakeholder submission documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination. The International Commission of Jurists, in a November 2024 UPR submission, listed LGBTIQ+ rights to equality and non-discrimination among its three principal concerns for the country.

There is no legal gender recognition. No statute provides a route to change the gender marker on official documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre concluded that section 4(1) of the Constitution, in its references to sex and other status, should be read to include gender identity in line with the UN Human Rights Committee, that no law permits a gender-marker change, and that a trans person travelling on a passport whose marker does not match their presentation could face a charge. Section 8(1) of the National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 requires the Director to take reasonable practicable steps to keep personal information in the Register complete, accurate and updated where necessary; a secondary source holds that this could be read to permit a marker change, but no procedure, eligibility criteria or granted-change outcomes are documented anywhere in the inventory.

Relationship recognition is restricted to opposite-sex couples. Under the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law, marriage is permitted only for opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised. Only married opposite-sex couples may adopt jointly, and single men and same-sex couples are barred from joint adoption. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex therefore has no recognised status.

The 2016 United States Department of State human rights report recorded that LGBTI persons faced societal discrimination and official insensitivity, that same-sex relationships were taboo and not openly discussed, and that no assaults were reported while incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma. The same report recorded the Matrix Support Group operating freely in all ten districts with a good working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service, including police intervention in December 2015 to enable a lesbian forced from home by her brothers to return, and a supportive police escort for a march of approximately 200 people from Lakeside to Central Park in Maseru on 21 May. The first gay pride march was held in central Maseru on 18 May 2013 with supportive authorities providing an escort, and marches have been held annually since, attracting a few hundred people.

The most recent dated incident in this inventory is the December 2015 police intervention and the 21 May march recorded in the 2016 report. The October 2024 submission records rape and assaults against LGBT people, but the inventory supplies no dates for those cases, and no later dated instance of violence is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The inventory carries a conflict on criminalisation. The 2016 United States Department of State report stated that the law at that time prohibited consensual sexual relations between men while authorities did not enforce it, and was silent on consensual sex between women. That snapshot conflicts with the 2012 decriminalisation recorded in the joint October 2024 UPR submission and should be read as a historical and unresolved discrepancy rather than the current rule.

The same 2016 report noted a June statement by Deputy Prime Minister Mothetjoa Metsing, made after the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS, that the government would look into decriminalising same-sex relationships to stop the spread of HIV. The inventory also describes Lesotho as having the second highest HIV prevalence in the world, with a figure of 25 percent of residents infected, cited without a date, and records LGBTQ activists reaching out to HIV-positive people with prevention strategies. The October 2024 joint submission separately documents barriers to health and education services for LGBT people.

The Southern African Litigation Centre, the People's Matrix Association and the Women's Law Centre briefing of October 2020 assessed Lesotho's law and policy on legal gender recognition against international best practice, and identified the Matrix as the only known LGBTI organisation in the country. The 2017 SALC constitutional analysis recorded that the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omitted gender and sexual orientation; the Labour Act 2024 has since added sexual orientation to the employment ground, leaving the gender omission unresolved in the inventory.

The International Commission of Jurists submission of November 2024 framed LGBTIQ+ equality and non-discrimination as one of three concerns, the others being inclusive education for children with disabilities and the revocation of practising certificates held by NGO lawyers.
localsOnly:
The Matrix Support Group, an LGBTI organisation established in 2009 and fully registered in 2010, works to build an environment where LGBTI people can freely express human rights and contribute socially, politically and economically regardless of gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation and sex, principally through engagement with partner organisations on gender-based violence. It includes transgender and intersex people. The 2016 United States Department of State report recorded its public outreach through film screenings, radio programmes, public gatherings, social media and an electronic billboard in central Maseru supporting LGBTI rights, and its operation in all ten districts.

Residents' workplace rights now rest on the Labour Act 2024, which covers unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, and prohibitions on forced and child labour, alongside the sexual-orientation ground and the workplace gender-based violence and harassment definition covering sex, gender and gender identity. The 2017 constitutional analysis found that the earlier Labour Code clause omitted gender and sexual orientation; the inventory does not state whether the 2024 Act's discrimination clause reaches gender identity beyond the violence and harassment definition.

Residents have no route to change a gender marker on official documents, no recognition of a relationship with a partner of the same legally recorded sex, and no access to joint adoption outside a marriage between a man and a woman. Children in the justice system have a statutory guarantee of non-discrimination on sexual orientation in the selection of a diversion programme under section 127(4) of the Children's Protection and Welfare Act 2011.

Pride marches have been held in Maseru every year since 18 May 2013, with supportive authorities providing an escort at the first march and at the march of approximately 200 people on 21 May recorded in the 2016 report.
outOfScopeNotes:
The reading of section 8(1) of the National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 as permitting a gender-marker change comes from a secondary source in the inventory. No procedure, eligibility criteria, penalty regime or documented instance of a granted change is sourced, so whether any marker change is achievable in practice is unresolved.

The inventory records no transgender-specific provisions on security screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention or gender-affirming care. Whether any such rules exist in Lesotho is not sourced either way.

The inventory contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. The only tolerance statement available is LGBTI-general, describing attitudes as slowly evolving, and it carries no figure or period.

The rape and assaults documented in the October 2024 joint stakeholder submission are undated in the inventory, so no recency can be established for them. Whether the Labour Act 2024 discrimination clause covers gender identity is not stated in the sources.

Claims drawn from the Wikipedia article on LGBTQ rights in Lesotho, including the marriage, adoption, credit-reporting and identity-card provisions, are not independently corroborated elsewhere in the inventory.
